sipha-maydis.summary: A glossy, almost black body makes this tiny aphid stand out among the greener insects on grasses. Wingless adults are roughly 1 to 2 millimeters long, with short antennae and stiff, spine-like hairs. Sipha maydis feeds on leaves and stems of cereals and other grasses, including wheat, barley, and corn, giving it a close connection to both crop fields and grassy vegetation.

sources.label: Argentina SENASA: Sipha maydis

tinocallis-ulmiparvifoliae.summary: Chinese elm is the plant to look at for this delicate aphid. Its winged adults are pale blue-green, with white wax stripes across the head and thorax and small waxy spots on the abdomen. At only about 2 millimeters long, these details need a close view; dark marks at the ends of some wing veins provide another useful identification clue.

sources.label: Blackman and Eastop: Aphids on the World's Plants

tuberocephalus-sakurae.summary: Curled, reddened cherry leaves can draw attention to this aphid before the insects themselves are visible. Adults and young shelter inside the distorted leaves, and an adult may be only about 1.5 millimeters long. Hokkaido forestry researchers describe this distinctive summer damage on flowering cherries, including the Japanese mountain cherry, making the leaf's shape an especially useful clue to its presence.

sources.label: Hokkaido Research Organization: Tuberocephalus sakurae

uroleucon-picridis.summary: Clusters of shiny reddish-brown aphids just below oxtongue flowers may belong to Uroleucon picridis. Wingless adults have dark antennae and dark rear tubes, contrasting with a yellow tail-like tip and paler bases to parts of the legs. Its strongest host association is with Picris plants; several records from other flower genera may involve similar aphids, so the host is a clue rather than a complete identification.

sources.label: Blackman and Eastop: Aphids on the World's Plants

aphidius-ervi.summary: This small black wasp spends its early life hidden inside an aphid. A female uses her antennae to inspect a potential host, then deposits an egg; the developing wasp leaves behind a swollen aphid mummy and eventually emerges through a round opening. Aphidius ervi is used in greenhouse biological control, where those mummies are a visible sign of its otherwise easily overlooked work.

sources.label: Kansas State University: Aphidius colemani and Aphidius ervi

aphis-pomi.summary: Apple aphids gather on tender new shoots, where their yellow-green bodies can blend into fresh foliage. They survive winter as shiny black eggs on twigs and fruit spurs, then build colonies as growth resumes. Heavy colonies can distort young shoots and leave sticky honeydew that supports sooty mold, although predators and other natural enemies often keep their numbers in check.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Green Apple Aphid

cassia-javanica.summary: Apple-blossom cassia is a tropical tree whose clusters of pink flowers soften toward paler shades as they age. Each compound leaf carries many paired leaflets, while the long, cylindrical pods reveal its membership in the bean family. Its showy flowers have made it a familiar ornamental, but the species includes several forms that botanists distinguish using small leaf-base structures and flower details.

sources.label: New York Botanical Garden: Cassia javanica monograph

cassia-javanica-var-indochinensis.summary: This form of apple-blossom cassia is associated with the pink-flowered trees widely grown in tropical gardens and streets. Its distinction from typical Cassia javanica rests mainly on smaller stipules at the leaf bases and shorter sepals around the flowers, rather than petal color. Botanical treatments differ in rank: the Bishop Museum places this older variety name under Cassia javanica subsp. agnes.

sources.label: New York Botanical Garden: Cassia javanica var. indochinensis
Bishop Museum: Cassia javanica subsp. agnes synonyms

phenacoccus-aceris.summary: A powdery white coat and a fringe of short waxy projections disguise the apple mealybug's darker, oval body. It feeds on tree leaves and branches, and a mature female produces a conspicuous white egg sac that largely covers her body. Beyond the insects themselves, sticky honeydew and the sooty mold it supports can make an infestation noticeable on orchard fruit and foliage.

sources.label: ScaleNet: Phenacoccus aceris
Washington State University: Apple Mealybug

mentha-suaveolens.summary: Apple mint has softly hairy, wrinkled leaves with toothed edges and a fruity mint scent. This creeping perennial favors damp places and sends up dense spikes of pink to white flowers above its foliage. Its familiar place in herb gardens can hide how readily it spreads in open ground, so a patch's expanding footprint is as characteristic as its aroma.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: Mentha suaveolens

nicandra-physalodes.summary: Sky-blue, cup-shaped flowers with white centers give apple of Peru a gardenlike appearance even when it grows among crops. This summer annual has hollow, strongly ridged stems and broad leaves with toothed or lobed edges. Papery coverings surround its many-seeded fruits; its escape from cultivation into soybean fields shows how an ornamental plant can become a persistent agricultural concern.

sources.label: Missouri State University: Apple-of-Peru

jasminum-sambac.summary: Arabian jasmine is a scrambling evergreen shrub or climber with glossy, broadly oval leaves and clusters of strongly scented white flowers. The blooms can become pink as they age, and cultivated forms include richly doubled flowers. Long grown for its fragrance, this jasmine supplies flowers used to scent tea; its botanical home is in tropical Asia, despite the geographic suggestion in its common name.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria: Jasminum sambac
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: Jasminum sambac

schismus-arabicus.summary: Arabian schismus is a small annual grass that forms low tufts with fine leaves and compact flower clusters in dry, open places. It reproduces by seed, and some plants break loose and tumble, scattering seed as they move. In desert shrubland, its dried growth can help carry fire between larger plants, although it closely resembles common Mediterranean grass and can be difficult to identify confidently.

sources.label: University of California Weed Research and Information Center: Mediterraneangrasses
California Invasive Plant Council: Schismus arabicus

brachyrhynchus-membranaceus.summary: This flat bug belongs to a group shaped for life in narrow spaces around decaying wood. Brachyrhynchus membranaceus feeds on fungal threads, linking it to the hidden community involved in wood decomposition. Its connection to fungi also matters commercially: researchers have reported damage to cultivated bracket fungi, showing that a small forest-associated insect can become troublesome when its food is grown as a crop.

sources.label: USDA ARS: Brachyrhynchus membranaceus research

neophyllaphis-araucariae.summary: Bright yellow to orange-yellow aphids on fresh Araucaria growth may be this tiny conifer specialist. Wingless adults are broad and oval, usually only about 1 to 1.5 millimeters long, so their host plant is an important first clue. Their association with young shoots makes the newest growth more informative to inspect than older foliage, while a close examination is still needed to separate similar insects.

sources.label: Blackman and Eastop: Aphids on the World's Plants

lindingaspis-rossi.summary: Araucaria black scale looks like a small, flat, dark disk attached to a leaf. The female's nearly circular cover is brown to black, with an especially dark spot close to its center where shed skins are incorporated. Despite its common name, this scale uses many kinds of plants, including oleander and citrus as well as Araucaria, so the host name alone does not define it.

sources.label: ScaleNet: Lindingaspis rossi

opuntia-leucotricha.summary: This pricklypear can grow into a branching shrub with a distinct trunk, giving it a small-tree silhouette. Its gray-green pads carry fine pale hairs and flexible white spines that can become especially conspicuous on older growth. Looking at the trunk, pad surface, and spines together is more useful than relying on the general pricklypear shape, which it shares with many other cacti.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Opuntia leucotricha

linepithema-humile.summary: Argentine ants are small, uniformly brown workers, often noticed as busy trails around gardens and buildings. Their colonies can contain many queens and linked nesting sites, sometimes supporting millions of ants. They nest in shallow soil and sheltered spaces beneath wood, mulch, or paving, which helps explain why a trail at one doorway may be only a small visible part of a much larger colony.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Argentine Ant

salvator-merianae.summary: The Argentine black and white tegu is a large South American lizard that can reach 4 to 5 feet long. Active by day, it eats a broad mix of fruit, invertebrates, small vertebrates, and eggs, and shelters in burrows during colder months. That flexible diet is central to concern about introduced populations, because native reptiles and ground-nesting wildlife can become part of its food supply.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Florida Invader, Tegu Lizard

lepidium-bonariense.summary: Argentine pepperweed is a modest mustard-family plant with hairy stems and finely divided lower leaves. Its tiny pale flowers give way to rounded, flattened seedpods with a small notch at the tip, often offering a clearer identification clue than the flowers. Lower leaves may already have fallen by flowering time, so young plants and mature fruiting stems can look surprisingly different.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Lepidium bonariense

aonidiella-taxus.summary: Aonidiella taxus hides beneath a pale, partly transparent scale cover about 2 millimeters across. The female beneath it changes from light brown toward reddish brown as she matures, while males develop narrower covers and eventually become winged adults. Associated with ornamental conifers, it can resemble several related scales, so a close view of the cover is useful for detection but microscopic features are needed for a confident species identification.

sources.label: Naturalis: Diaspididae of the World, Aonidiella taxus

dynaspidiotus-pseudomeyeri.summary: False Meyer scale forms slightly raised, oval to irregularly round covers that change from dull greenish yellow to a dirtier pale yellow with brown edging. Its recorded hosts include junipers, false cypresses, and arborvitae. Those subdued colors make it an unobtrusive resident of ornamental conifers, although researchers have documented damaging infestations; its resemblance to other scales makes careful identification more useful than judging by color alone.

sources.label: ScaleNet: Dynaspidiotus pseudomeyeri

gymnaspis-aechmeae.summary: Known as flyspeck scale, this insect is especially associated with bromeliads and greenhouse plants. A young female has a brown cover with a dark shed skin, while the adult remains enclosed within the skin of her previous growth stage. Females produce living young rather than simply depositing eggs, and damaging populations on ornamental bromeliads make these easily overlooked specks worth recognizing.

sources.label: ScaleNet: Gymnaspis aechmeae

howardia-biclavis.summary: Mining scale can be hard to see because plant tissue partly conceals its rounded protective cover. It lives on the bark of many woody plants, with a pale white or yellow cover and a brownish spot formed from earlier shed skins. The name should not be taken as proof that it actively tunnels: published accounts disagree about how it becomes covered by the plant's outer tissue.

sources.label: ScaleNet: Howardia biclavis

lepidosaphes-pinnaeformis.summary: Small brown scales shaped like mussel shells on orchid leaves may be Lepidosaphes pinnaeformis. It favors orchids, although records include other plants, and sometimes settles on stems as well as foliage. Heavy colonies can leave discolored patches around feeding sites and spoil the leaves' appearance; the mobile young spread within plants, while movement of infested orchids can carry established colonies much farther.

sources.label: Naturalis: Diaspididae of the World, Lepidosaphes pinnaeformis

lepidosaphes-yanagicola.summary: Firebush scale forms narrow brown covers shaped like tiny oyster shells, with pale bodies hidden underneath. Fertilized females survive winter on their host plants, and the next generation begins as small mobile crawlers. Covers are usually straight but may bend when crowded; on heavily infested plants, scales can also occur near leaf midveins, making both woody growth and foliage useful places to look.

sources.label: University of Massachusetts Amherst: Lepidosaphes yanagicola

neopinnaspis-harperi.summary: Harper scale blends into bark so well that even dense colonies can escape notice. Its narrow, nearly flat tan covers are only 1 to 2 millimeters long, with darker shed skins gathered at one end and a pink or red female beneath. It settles especially in bark cracks on a wide range of woody hosts, including cotoneaster, ceanothus, and macadamia.

sources.label: Naturalis: Diaspididae of the World, Neopinnaspis harperi

parlatoria-camelliae.summary: Camellia parlatoria scale forms small white to gray oval covers, each with a darker area in the incorporated shed skin. It is named for camellia but has been recorded from a much wider assortment of plants. Observations on camellia found males and females on both leaf surfaces, often near veins, so a pale speck beside a vein may deserve a closer look.

sources.label: ScaleNet: Parlatoria camelliae

rutherfordia-major.summary: Lychee bark scale has a white protective cover that may look reddish brown or nearly black when plant tissue obscures it. The cover is rounded to oval, with brown shed skins near its edge. Although lychee gives this insect one of its common names, recorded hosts include other tropical trees and shrubs; its concealed appearance can make the living insect less obvious than the raised patch it creates.

sources.label: ScaleNet: Rutherfordia major

selenaspidus-albus.summary: This small armored scale forms a circular white cover about 1.75 millimeters across, marked by yellowish-brown shed skins slightly off center. Published records associate it with Euphorbia plants, where the pale disks can build into dense populations. Its simple appearance is a useful first clue, but it belongs to a group of similar-looking insects whose species distinctions depend on much finer anatomical details.

sources.label: ScaleNet: Selenaspidus albus

selenaspidus-articulatus.summary: Selenaspidus articulatus forms flat, partly transparent disks with pale margins and a darker spot near the center. It often gathers on the sun-facing upper surfaces of leaves and uses many host plants, with citrus especially favored. Dense colonies can cause yellowing and tissue damage on leaves and fruit, connecting an insect that looks like a tiny surface blemish with a much larger effect on plant health.

sources.label: Naturalis: Diaspididae of the World, Selenaspidus articulatus

unaspis-citri.summary: The snowy coating that gives citrus snow scale its name is made by the white covers of immature males. Females are less conspicuous, living beneath darker armor, and colonies mainly occupy trunks and larger limbs of citrus trees. Heavy, persistent infestations can weaken trees and contribute to bark splitting; the contrasting male and female covers are a reminder that one species can have very different appearances.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Citrus Snow Scale

andaspis-punicae.summary: This scale's long, narrow cover resembles a dark mussel shell, sometimes edged with a whitish deposit. Known in older literature as Andaspis punicae and now placed in Lepidosaphes, it is associated with woody hosts including lychee. Researchers have linked heavy infestations with declining tree vigor and branch dieback, making an insect that can pass for part of the bark relevant to tropical fruit growers.

sources.label: ScaleNet: Lepidosaphes punicae
USDA ARS: Andaspis punicae in lychee

fiorinia-proboscidaria.summary: Snout scale has a glossy golden-brown, lance-shaped cover with a raised ridge down the middle. The adult female remains within an enlarged shed skin, and colonies can contain several life stages together on the undersides of leaves. Citrus is an important host, but close relatives look much alike, so recognizing the general shape is only a first step toward identifying this particular scale.

sources.label: ScaleNet: Fiorinia proboscidaria

dichrostachys-cinerea.summary: Aroma is a thorny shrub or small tree with finely divided leaves and especially distinctive hanging flower heads. Each head combines a yellow tip of fertile flowers with a pink or mauve section of sterile flowers, followed by crowded, twisted seed pods. Short side branches end in sharp spines, and suckering growth can produce thickets, giving this delicate-looking plant a much tougher presence than its flowers suggest.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Dichrostachys cinerea

paspalum-paniculatum.summary: Arrocillo is a coarse perennial grass that grows in substantial clumps, with broad, flat leaves and flowering stems that can rise above a person's waist. Its seed head has many slender branches spreading from a central stalk, each carrying closely arranged, rounded spikelets. Found in settings such as forest clearings and plantations, it is best recognized by that branching seed head rather than by its otherwise ordinary grass leaves.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Paspalum paniculatum

pseudosasa-japonica.summary: Arrow bamboo forms dense stands of upright canes topped with long, broad, glossy green leaves. Underground stems extend beyond the clump and send up new shoots, allowing a planting to occupy more ground over time. Its leaves can reach roughly a foot long, giving the stand a lush, leafy appearance; naturalized populations have been documented along roadsides, riverbanks, and forest edges after escape from gardens.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Pseudosasa japonica

xanthosoma-sagittifolium.summary: Arrowleaf elephant's ear is a large tropical herb with long stalks supporting broad, arrow-shaped leaves above a thickened stem. The stalk joins the leaf at its base, a useful detail when comparing plants commonly called elephant's ears. It grows in shaded, moist settings such as forest understory and streambanks, and its flowers sit on a fleshy spike partly enclosed by a boat-shaped bract.

sources.label: Singapore NParks: Xanthosoma sagittifolium

caladium-bicolor.summary: Artist's pallet is a tuberous tropical plant grown for leaves that can combine green, white, pink, and red in striking patterns. The leaf stalk attaches within the blade rather than simply at its edge, and the broad leaves range from heart-shaped to arrow-shaped. Its small flowers are crowded onto a fleshy spike inside a pale bract, but the colorful foliage is usually what draws attention in a garden.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Caladium bicolor

diplosoma-listerianum.summary: This ascidian is a colony of tiny marine animals living together in a thin, shared outer covering. Each individual draws seawater through its own inlet, filters food from it, and releases the water through an opening shared with neighbors. Colonies grow across submerged surfaces such as docks, floats, and boat hulls, where their spreading sheets are part of the living community commonly described as marine fouling.

sources.label: Smithsonian NEMESIS: Diplosoma listerianum

polyandrocarpa-zorritensis.summary: This colonial sea squirt forms groups of small, club-shaped individuals connected at their bases by rootlike strands. Each animal has its own tough outer covering, often coated with sand, and two openings used to move water through its filtering apparatus. Colonies expand by budding as well as reproducing sexually; their clustered shape helps distinguish them from ascidians that spread as flat sheets over submerged surfaces.

sources.label: Smithsonian NEMESIS: Polyandrocarpa zorritensis

siphoninus-phillyreae.summary: Ash whitefly is a sap-feeding insect whose adults carry a light dusting of white wax. On leaf undersides, the settled immature stages are more distinctive: their tiny cases bear white wax tufts and glassy projections tipped with wax droplets. Despite its name, it feeds on many ornamental and fruit trees, and heavy infestations can cause wilting, early leaf loss, and smaller fruit.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Ash Whitefly

potentilla-inclinata.summary: Ashy cinquefoil is a perennial herb with upright or ascending, softly hairy stems and small yellow flowers. Its leaves divide into five to seven deeply toothed leaflets, pale green above and grayish with hairs beneath, giving the plant its ashy appearance. It grows in dry, sandy grassland and disturbed places such as roadsides and railway banks; the leaflet shape and hairs help separate it from similar cinquefoils.

sources.label: German Federal Agency for Nature Conservation FloraWeb: Potentilla inclinata

sphaerodactylus-elegans.summary: Ashy gecko is a tiny lizard whose appearance changes dramatically with age: brightly banded young with reddish tails become tan or rusty brown adults covered in pale speckles. It favors moist hiding places in leaf litter, beneath bark, and among wood or rocks, often near buildings. Although much of its life is spent close to the ground, it also climbs fences and trees while searching for small prey.

sources.label: Heagy and Frank, The Reef Geckos of Florida, Iguana (2008)

eriocaulon-cinereum.summary: Ashy pipewort is a small annual that forms a tight tuft of narrow, pointed leaves close to the ground. Slender stalks rise above the tuft, each ending in a tiny rounded flower head colored gray, straw brown, or darker brown. It grows along drying pool margins and seepages, and has also become associated with rice cultivation, where its buttonlike heads help distinguish it from young grasses.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Eriocaulon cinereum

polypogon-fugax.summary: Asia minor bluegrass is a small annual grass that may grow upright or bend near the ground, sometimes rooting at its lower joints. Its flowering head is a dense, narrow cluster whose tiny spikelets carry short, fine bristles, giving it a softer outline than strongly bristly relatives. Rough leaf surfaces and the compact seed head are useful features to examine when separating it from other short grasses.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Polypogon fugax

aedes-japonicus.summary: Asian bush mosquito has golden stripes across its upper body and contrasting pale bands on dark legs. Its larvae develop in small pools held by tree holes, rocks, discarded tires, and other containers, and can remain active in cooler conditions than many related mosquitoes. Adults feed on plant sugars, while females also take blood meals, making this container-breeding species relevant around homes as well as woodland edges.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Asian Bush Mosquito

dryocosmus-kuriphilus.summary: Asian chestnut gall wasp is usually noticed through the rounded green or pink swellings it produces on chestnut buds, leaves, and young shoots. Tiny larvae shelter inside these galls, which later dry into brown, woody structures that can remain on the tree. Females reproduce without mating, and repeated gall formation can disrupt shoot growth and flowering, reducing tree vigor and the production of chestnuts.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Asian Chestnut Gall Wasp

diaphorina-citri.summary: Asian citrus psyllid is a tiny mottled brown insect that feeds with its rear end tilted upward, almost like a thorn projecting from a citrus leaf. Its yellowish young gather on tender new growth and produce conspicuous curly tubes of white wax. Feeding can distort shoots, but its greater significance is its ability to spread bacteria associated with huanglongbing, also called citrus greening, a destructive disease of citrus trees.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Asian Citrus Psyllid and Huanglongbing Disease

blattella-asahinai.summary: Asian cockroach closely resembles the familiar German cockroach, but has longer wings and is a strong flier. It primarily lives outdoors in shaded mulch, compost, and accumulated plant litter, becoming active around sundown and flying toward brightly lit areas. Adults may enter buildings through doors or windows, although indoor infestations are uncommon; recognizing its outdoor habits helps explain why one might suddenly appear near a light.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Asian Cockroach
